payer: the holder of a Binance dated (quarterly) futures contract, force-delivered at a published index average on a calendar minute
why_they_keep_paying: Delivery price is a mechanical per-second average of the index over a fixed clock window before 08:00 UTC on the last Friday of the quarter (07:00-08:00 for the whole 2019-2024 period; shortened to 07:30-08:00 only on 2024-11-11), and the contract goes Reduce-Only 10 minutes before delivery, so the holder can neither choose an exit price nor re-open. Anyone who wants the exposure to continue past expiry must roll on the exchange's calendar rather than their own.
what_would_end_it: Retirement of dated contracts in favour of continuously rolling ones, or a settlement defined on a price the holder can actually transact against (a closing auction) instead of a backward-looking average during a window in which they are locked out.
observable: In 1-minute perpetual bars, the 07:00-08:00 UTC hour of the last Friday of March, June, September and December should differ from the same hour on ordinary Fridays and on the last Friday of non-quarter months - in intrabar range, in signed drift across the hour, and in what happens to that move after 08:00. The footprint should exist only for the assets that actually had a listed dated contract (BTC, ETH), leaving the several hundred alt perps as a within-venue, same-minute control.
needs_data_we_lack: prices and open interest of the dated quarterly contracts themselves; the Binance index price series used for settlement; off-venue option expiry open interest, which shares the same 08:00 UTC fixing convention and would be needed to attribute the flow rather than merely detect it
distinct_from: The payment is a fixing on a calendar the exchange publishes and is owed by any holder of a dated contract irrespective of side or leverage, whereas every closed family is paid per 8-hour settlement by whoever stands on the crowded side of a perpetual.

payer: the holder of a large position in a named symbol whose margin tiers Binance has announced it will tighten at a stated timestamp
why_they_keep_paying: Binance unilaterally rewrites the notional-to-maintenance-margin ladder for individual symbols with a few days' notice and states plainly that existing positions are affected and must be reduced before the effective minute or face liquidation - MTLUSDT's top tier, for example, was moved so that 1x and 50% maintenance margin began at 4m instead of 6m USDT. The ladder exists to cap the exchange's own tail risk, so it keeps being tightened precisely in the symbols whose inventory is hardest to exit.
what_would_end_it: Grandfathering positions opened under the old ladder, or cross-symbol portfolio margining that stops the constraint from binding symbol by symbol.
observable: In the affected symbol alone, the minutes before the announced effective timestamp should carry one-sided forced reduction - abnormal volume and abnormal range against whichever side is large - with neighbouring symbols and the same clock time on adjacent days as controls. Nothing should show up in that symbol's funding history, because the payment is not a funding settlement; that absence is itself the discriminator.
needs_data_we_lack: the archive of Binance leverage- and margin-tier change announcements with their effective timestamps, and the historical per-symbol margin-tier tables. Neither is in the 1-minute panel, the funding history or the listing/delisting table; both would have to be collected from the exchange's announcement pages before the mechanism could be measured at all.
distinct_from: This is a scheduled, pre-announced deleveraging forced by a rulebook change rather than by price, so the payer is identified by position size in one named symbol at one announced minute - not by being the crowded funding-payer, and not by being margin-called in a cascade.

payer: the trader whose futures collateral is a private stablecoin that the venue values at exactly 1.0000 USD and who holds no par-redemption right of their own
why_they_keep_paying: Margin, PnL and liquidation on a USDⓈ-M contract are all computed in the quote stablecoin at a hard one-dollar peg, while the actual 1:1 redemption right sits only with onboarded customers of the issuer - Paxos guaranteed BUSD redemption to onboarded customers through at least February 2024, and Binance later force-converted leftover BUSD futures balances to USDT on its own timetable starting 2023-12-14. The venue offers no dollar rail, so the marginal trader cannot opt out of holding issuer credit as the unit of account.
what_would_end_it: Collateral marked at its traded price rather than at par, native USD or tokenised-treasury margin, or an on-venue redemption facility open to every holder rather than to onboarded issuer clients.
observable: This venue ran perps on the same asset quoted in different stablecoins side by side - BTCUSDT against BTCBUSD, ETHUSDT against ETHBUSD, and later USDC-quoted pairs. If the mechanism is real, the same-minute price ratio between such a pair steps within a single minute during peg stress and around the announced wind-down dates, and - unlike a funding differential, which drifts smoothly - that step is simultaneous and same-signed across every symbol sharing the quote asset, which is a cross-sectional signature no per-symbol basis can imitate.
needs_data_we_lack: confirmation that 1-minute bars for the BUSD-quoted and USDC-quoted USDⓈ-M perps are actually in the archive (the BUSD contracts were settled and delisted 2023-12-08 and 2023-12-11 and may simply be absent), plus an off-venue stablecoin/USD price such as USDT/USD or BUSD/USD spot elsewhere, without which one can only say the two legs diverged and not which leg moved
distinct_from: The payment is on the collateral's unit of account and is owed by longs and shorts alike, including a perfectly delta-hedged book with no directional exposure at all, whereas every closed family requires a directional perpetual position and is paid through the funding settlement.

payer: the holder of an open position in a perp Binance has announced it will retire, and the spot-versus-perp hedger who loses their only shortable leg on the exchange's date
why_they_keep_paying: Binance routinely retires low-liquidity contracts on roughly a week's notice, suspends trading and switches to reduce-only shortly before the cutoff, then closes every remaining position by automatic settlement at an index average the holder cannot transact against - the exchange states that its settlement-price rule covers delisting-subject contracts as well as delivery contracts. For many of these tokens the perp was the only venue where the exposure could be shorted at all, so a hedged holder must unwind the entire structure on a date the venue chose.
what_would_end_it: Longer notice, positions made transferable into a replacement contract, or settlement referenced to a deep spot venue instead of a thin index on a dying token.
observable: The project already holds the listing/delisting table, so the final sessions of the delisted symbols can be aligned on their own clock rather than on wall-clock time: 1-minute bars should show volume collapsing while intrabar range widens, a signed drift through the last hours, and a discontinuity at the announced settlement hour that symbols still listed on those same dates never display.
needs_data_we_lack: the announcement (notice) date and the exact settlement timestamp for each historical delisting - the held table records the delisting date, not when the venue told anyone - plus the index price used at settlement. KT-3 already found that only 481 of 986 symbols ever traded have bars locally and 266 are delisted, so the honest risk is that the aligned ensemble is too small to support any statement, and that should be checked before anything is registered.
distinct_from: The constraint here is the venue withdrawing the instrument itself on a published date, which extracts payment from both legs of a hedge and from shorts as readily as longs, so it depends on neither crowding nor leverage nor the funding rate; it is also not a basket claim - each delisting is its own dated event, though the sample of such events is exactly what KT-3 says is thin.

payer: a leveraged Binance USD-M perpetual short whose collateral has fallen below maintenance margin
why_they_keep_paying: Binance removes the trader's discretion and submits an Immediate-or-Cancel order to buy back the short, while also charging a liquidation-clearance fee. The constraint is the exchange's maintenance-margin and liquidation protocol, not a voluntary reaction to price.
what_would_end_it: The forced payment would stop if the position were closed or recapitalized before breaching maintenance margin, or if Binance replaced market liquidation with a mechanism that did not execute the position against the market.
observable: If forced short covering has a material footprint, sharp upward one-minute moves should exhibit asymmetric continuation and elevated volume, followed by relaxation once the compulsory buy flow is exhausted.
needs_data_we_lack: Binance liquidation-order records or forced-order stream, mark-price bars, account leverage and collateral, and open interest are needed to distinguish forced short covering from ordinary aggressive buying.
distinct_from: The payer is a liquidated short forced to buy into an upward move, not a funding-paying leveraged long or a liquidated long selling into a cascade.

payer: a short-gamma BTC or ETH options dealer executing compulsory delta rebalancing through Binance USD-M perpetuals
why_they_keep_paying: The dealer's outstanding option liability and delta-risk limit require buying as the underlying rises and selling as it falls, especially as gamma concentrates near expiry. This flow persists because abandoning the hedge would violate the dealer's inventory-risk constraint.
what_would_end_it: The pressure ends when the options expire or are closed, the dealer's net gamma becomes non-negative, or the hedge is moved away from Binance perpetuals.
observable: Binance BTCUSDT or ETHUSDT one-minute bars could show increased volume and same-direction price acceleration during the 07:30-08:00 UTC Deribit expiry window, followed by reversal after the expiring exposure and its hedge disappear.
needs_data_we_lack: Options open interest by strike and expiry, dealer-position or gamma estimates, and venue-level hedge-flow data are required to identify the sign and magnitude of the compulsory hedge rather than merely testing a calendar footprint.
distinct_from: The payer is an options intermediary constrained by nonlinear inventory exposure, and the payment is adverse hedge execution rather than perpetual funding or long-side liquidation.

payer: the profitable, highly leveraged USDⓈ-M perpetual holder whose winning position is force-closed by auto-deleveraging at the bankrupt counterparty's bankruptcy price
why_they_keep_paying: Binance ranks the ADL queue by the product of percentage P&L and leverage and closes the queued position at the losing trader's bankruptcy price whenever a contract's insurance fund cannot accept a bankrupt position; there is no opt-out and the only way to leave the front of the queue is to be less right or less levered. Insurance-fund depth is finite while position size on thin symbols is not, so the exchange's own rulebook guarantees the payment recurs.
what_would_end_it: a balance-sheet guarantee deep enough to absorb every bankruptcy — Binance has already published one for BTC, ETH and BNB USDⓈ-M below a stated open-interest level, which is exactly why the payment survives only in the symbols that guarantee does not reach.
observable: on thin symbols during cascade minutes, a burst of prints far from the contemporaneous majors followed by an immediate snap-back, with that minute's high-low range far exceeding what the move in BTC/ETH implies; the winning side's exposure vanishes in the same minute as the losing side's, so the reversal is symmetric rather than one-directional like an ordinary liquidation sweep.
needs_data_we_lack: ADL event notifications, per-contract insurance-fund balance history, open interest, and trade prints — 1-minute OHLCV alone cannot separate an ADL wave from ordinary forced closing.
distinct_from: the payer here is the trader who was right, expropriated because of profit and leverage, not the leveraged long paying funding nor the under-margined holder being liquidated.

payer: the Binance Dual Investment subscriber, locked until settlement, whose payoff is decided by an average of the market price over the 30 minutes before 08:00 UTC
why_they_keep_paying: Product terms state the subscription cannot be edited, cancelled or redeemed before the settlement date, so the subscriber has sold optionality they hold no right to buy back, and the fixing is a mechanically computed average over a pre-announced fixed-clock window rather than a price anyone chooses. The product is re-issued with new tenors every day, so the same lock-up and the same 07:30–08:00 UTC window recur daily rather than at an event.
what_would_end_it: granting an early-redemption right, or moving to a settlement reference that is not a pre-announced fixed-clock average — a randomised observation minute would remove the whole constraint.
observable: the 07:30–08:00 UTC half-hour should behave unlike any other half-hour of the day in 1-minute bars: different internal range shape, different volume distribution, and a different tendency to revert immediately after 08:00. Critically, the effect should be confined to the handful of assets Binance actually issues these products on (BTC, ETH, BNB and a few majors) and absent across the rest of the 480-symbol panel — a market-wide 08:00 UTC effect would falsify it as a session artefact.
needs_data_we_lack: outstanding notional and strike distribution of Binance's structured-product book, and the spot index series that defines the fixing; the project holds perp bars only.
distinct_from: the payer is a locked retail yield-product subscriber bound by a fixed-clock averaging window and a no-redemption clause — not a dealer rebalancing continuously against gamma, and the dealer facing this book is on the opposite side of the option from the notebook's short-gamma entry.

payer: the Binance USDⓈ-M futures liquidity-provider-program participant whose next week's maker rebate tier is set by its share of Monday-to-Sunday maker volume
why_they_keep_paying: The tier is recomputed automatically every Tuesday around 04:00 UTC from the Monday 00:00 to Sunday 23:59 UTC week, the weekly review scores bid/offer spread, order size, order duration and market-making time, and three consecutive unqualified weeks removes the account with a one-month bar on reapplying. Because the rebate then applies to the participant's entire book while the cost of defending the rank is confined to the marginal volume it adds, quoting through windows it would otherwise skip stays rational for them indefinitely.
what_would_end_it: replacing share-of-total ranking with an absolute threshold, continuous rather than weekly measurement, or an explicit per-symbol depth obligation — any of the three removes the weekly cliff that makes the marginal volume worth buying.
observable: a weekly periodicity anchored to the Monday 00:00 UTC boundary that is not a day-of-week volatility effect: 1-minute mean reversion and the concentration of volume within the day should drift across the week and reset at the boundary, with the effect largest on thin symbols where one participant's volume can actually move a share ranking and absent on BTC and ETH where it cannot.
needs_data_we_lack: the maker/taker split of volume and any per-account attribution; from OHLCV bars a participant's volume share is not recoverable, so only the aggregate weekly signature is testable.
distinct_from: the payer is a fee-tier-ranked liquidity provider spending on a calendar deadline written into an exchange incentive schedule; nothing about its position is levered, funded or margin-constrained.

payer: the USDⓈ-M perpetual holder whose order-entry path degrades while the venue's own risk engine keeps closing positions
why_they_keep_paying: A perp position exists only inside one matching engine and is not portable, so there is no substitute exit when order entry fails, and the exchange's stated compensation posture covers realised losses from system issues rather than exits that could not be taken. Capacity is provisioned for normal load, which means the failure is correlated with the exact minutes an exit is worth most — the documented case is 19 May 2021, roughly 12:40 to 13:10 UTC, when futures users could not exit while forced closures continued.
what_would_end_it: portability of the position through cross-venue portfolio margining or clearing, or a published rule that suspends the liquidation engine whenever order entry is degraded — either removes the asymmetry rather than the outage.
observable: the only candidate here measurable entirely from the held panel: 1-minute bars missing simultaneously across the whole USDⓈ-M cross-section, or collapsing to a frozen last price, during a large move — followed by a reopen gap. The panel's own gap structure dates and sizes every episode, and because Binance runs spot and futures on separate matching engines the signature should be futures-wide rather than tied to any one symbol.
needs_data_we_lack: an authoritative exchange incident and status timeline; without it a run of missing minutes cannot be told apart from a hole in the vendor archive, which is the failure mode that would make this mechanism look real when it is not.
distinct_from: the binding constraint is venue availability, not margin level — this payer can be fully collateralised and still unable to act, and the party collecting is whoever could still transact.

payer: the Binance Leveraged Token hedge basket that must restore its mandated leverage through underlying perpetual contracts
why_they_keep_paying: Each leveraged token represents a basket of perpetual positions, and its leverage mandate requires exposure to increase after favorable moves and decrease after adverse moves. Rebalancing therefore compels same-direction trading after sufficiently large moves regardless of execution cost.
what_would_end_it: Discontinuation of the leveraged-token product, removal of the relevant perpetual from its basket, or replacement of the leverage-restoration mandate
observable: Abnormally high minute volume and same-sign return continuation following large underlying moves, concentrated in symbols represented by Binance Leveraged Tokens
needs_data_we_lack: Historical leveraged-token NAV, AUM, target leverage, basket composition, and exact rebalance timestamps
distinct_from: The payer is a product-level hedge portfolio obeying a leverage mandate, not a funding-paying long, a liquidated trader, or any payer already in the notebook.

payer: the Binance USDⓈ-M Futures copy trader whose account automatically duplicates a lead trader's close
why_they_keep_paying: Binance automatically converts copied closes into market orders after the lead order fills, and copied exits have no slippage protection. The follower keeps accepting that concession because synchronized execution is the service they delegated to the platform.
what_would_end_it: Ending the copy relationship or changing copied closes to independently priced, slippage-capped orders
observable: A lead trader's price-moving fill should be followed by an immediate second wave in the same direction as follower market closes arrive, producing concentrated minute volume and short-horizon continuation
needs_data_we_lack: Lead-trader fill timestamps, copied follower count and AUM, and order-level attribution of copied market closes
distinct_from: This payer incurs execution slippage because of automatic trade replication, not funding, liquidation, ADL, expiry, delisting, or a margin-rule change.

payer: the Binance USDⓈ-M TWAP user who has committed a large order to a finite completion window
why_they_keep_paying: Binance's TWAP service automatically releases pieces at regular intervals, while its duration and quantity constraints can force execution attempts before the window ends. A user with an external completion mandate cannot simply wait indefinitely for passive fills when price moves against the order.
what_would_end_it: Removal of the completion deadline, cancellation of the algorithm, or permission to leave the parent order unfinished indefinitely
observable: Sustained one-sided minute returns accompanied by elevated volume over a bounded interval, with pressure recurring at regular subintervals until the parent order ends
needs_data_we_lack: TWAP parent-order direction, start and end times, requested quantity, child-order timestamps, and completion status
distinct_from: The payer is an execution-deadline-constrained parent order rather than a funding participant, liquidated position, scheduled settlement holder, or previously listed venue-rule payer.

payer: the Binance USDⓈ-M derivatives user resident in a jurisdiction Binance has announced it is exiting, whose remaining open positions are force-closed by the venue at a published wall-clock deadline
why_they_keep_paying: The deadline is set by a licensing outcome the user has no part in, and Binance removes the ability to close manually at the stated timestamp before closing whatever is left, so the exit is decided by a calendar rather than by price or by the holder's view. It recurs because Binance's registration status keeps changing country by country, and each exit follows the same template: no new or increased positions, a fixed wind-down window, then venue-executed closure.
what_would_end_it: Binance holding local derivatives permissions everywhere it has users, or offboarding by transferring open positions to a licensed affiliate instead of closing them into the book.
observable: A one-directional imbalance appearing simultaneously across a very large number of symbols in the same minute, anchored to a published UTC deadline rather than to any symbol's own news, with no accompanying change in that symbol's funding history; and elevated turnover distributed across the preceding 90-day wind-down window rather than concentrated at its start. Confirmed events inside the project's data range include 2021-12-23 23:59 UTC (Australia) and 2021-07-30 + 90 days (Germany, Italy, Netherlands), plus the 2023-07-17 00:00 UTC Netherlands withdrawal-only cutover.
needs_data_we_lack: The archive of Binance offboarding announcements with exact deadline timestamps and affected product sets, and any measure of the affected cohort's size — per-jurisdiction open interest or account counts are not public, so bar data alone cannot say whether a cohort was large enough to leave a mark.
distinct_from: The payer is defined by residency and a regulator's decision, not by leverage, margin health or funding, and the forced flow lands on every symbol at one timestamp rather than on one symbol at its own retirement date.

payer: the holder of a CME-cleared bitcoin or ether futures obligation priced off the CME CF Reference Rate, whose offsetting leg sits in a Binance USDⓈ-M perpetual
why_they_keep_paying: CME's crypto futures are cash-settled to a benchmark fixed inside the 15:00–16:00 London hour on a published expiry calendar (last Friday of the contract month), and BTIC transactions are struck explicitly as a differential to that same fix, so the hedger's realised price on one leg is decided by a clock they do not control. Binance is not a constituent exchange of that benchmark, so the perpetual leg cannot be priced by the fix and has to be moved inside the window on Binance's own tape, at whatever that window costs.
what_would_end_it: CF Benchmarks admitting Binance to the constituent set, CME moving to a continuously-observed settlement, or the hedge leg migrating onto a venue that is inside the index.
observable: Calendar-locked intensity in BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT 1-minute bars during 15:00–16:00 London on CME expiry days, absent on non-expiry Fridays and absent in symbols with no CME contract; within that hour, structure aligned to the benchmark's twelve five-minute partitions rather than smoothly distributed; and a distinct signature at the expiry minute itself versus the rest of the window.
needs_data_we_lack: The CME expiry calendar and the published BRR/ETHUSD_RR fixings, needed both to align the windows and to measure the perpetual against the benchmark it is not part of. The project holds no order book, trade prints or open interest, so only bar-level volume, range and close location are available inside the window.
distinct_from: The binding constraint is a different exchange's settlement calendar and a benchmark Binance does not belong to, so the payment falls due whether the holder is long or short and regardless of what funding is doing; it is not the Binance quarterly holder settled on Binance's own index at 08:00 UTC.

payer: the Binance USDⓈ-M perpetual holder whose position is closed by the venue on a Mark Price built from other exchanges' spot feeds, when one of those feeds stalls or dislocates
why_they_keep_paying: Binance computes the Price Index as a weighted average of external spot venues, caps any single venue at ±3% from the median (±1% for BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, SOLUSDT, XRPUSDT and the other named majors), and sets a venue's weight to zero once its data is five minutes stale — and the resulting Mark Price, not Binance's own traded price, is what decides liquidation. The holder cannot opt out of it, cannot trade the index directly, and learns the index moved only after it has already moved against them.
what_would_end_it: Binance pricing closures off its own tape, or the index becoming broad and deep enough that one constituent's outage or dislocation cannot shift the weighted average before the stale-feed rule fires.
observable: Minute bars in which a symbol's own traded range does not contain the excursion that would have been required to close positions at the printed extreme — an abrupt one-minute move and near-complete reversion, carrying the volume asymmetry of forced closes rather than of two-sided trading, and clustering in symbols whose index is built from few venues rather than in the majors that carry the tighter cap. If real, the same minute should show nothing unusual in the funding history.
needs_data_we_lack: The Index Price and Mark Price series, the per-venue constituent list and weights over time (Binance exposes constituents via GET /fapi/v1/constituents but the project holds none of it), and liquidation prints. Without those the excursion is visible but not attributable to the index rule rather than to ordinary illiquidity.
distinct_from: The trigger is an outage or price dislocation on a venue the holder never traded on, so it reaches a fully-margined position as readily as a stretched one and hits longs and shorts symmetrically — the constraint is the venue's pricing rulebook, not the holder's leverage, margin shortfall or funding bill.

payer: the BNB Launchpool participant who shorts BNBUSDT perpetuals while retaining reward-eligible BNB
why_they_keep_paying: Launchpool rewards accrue according to the participant's eligible BNB balance, so selling the BNB sacrifices the allocation. A perpetual hedge preserves that eligibility while transferring BNB price risk, making hedge carry and execution costs an economically durable payment.
what_would_end_it: Launchpool and related BNB-balance rewards ending, eligibility no longer requiring BNB exposure, or a cheaper hedge becoming available
observable: BNBUSDT perpetual volume and selling pressure after Launchpool announcements or farming starts, followed by hedge reductions around farming ends; funding may become less positive or negative while hedges are outstanding
needs_data_we_lack: historical Launchpool announcement, start and end timestamps; eligible BNB pool balances; participant-level hedge positions
distinct_from: The payer is a reward-eligible spot-BNB holder buying insurance against required inventory exposure, not a leveraged directional long or a trader harvesting the opposite side of funding.

payer: the registered Binance Futures tournament entrant trading to satisfy a daily volume qualification or leaderboard tie-break
why_they_keep_paying: Published tournament rules condition prize eligibility, voting rights, and some ranking tie-breaks on futures volume measured inside fixed UTC windows. Entrants therefore continue paying fees and spread when additional turnover has contest value even if it has little standalone trading value.
what_would_end_it: The qualification window closing, the entrant becoming unable to improve eligibility or rank, or Binance removing volume-conditioned rewards
observable: Elevated perpetual volume near daily 00:00 UTC qualification resets and tournament endpoints, with the excess disappearing after the published promotion period; OHLC ranges may rise if deadline-driven taker flow consumes liquidity
needs_data_we_lack: a complete historical calendar of USD-M-eligible tournaments, participant registrations, leaderboard states, and maker-versus-taker volume
distinct_from: The payer is an incentive-qualified contest entrant generating deadline-bound turnover, not a funding payer, liquidated position, copy trader, TWAP user, or liquidity-provider-program participant.

payer: a token market maker that sold borrowed project tokens under a loan-and-call agreement and must redeliver them in kind at a fixed contract expiry
why_they_keep_paying: The loan-and-call structure is the standard way a project pays for listing liquidity: the MM receives roughly 1-5% of circulating supply as a 12-24 month loan, with a call struck about 25-100% above the TGE price, and at expiry it must either return the same number of tokens or exercise. If the token is below the strike on that date the option is worthless, so redelivery in kind is compulsory and an MM that already sold the inventory has to buy it back on a date fixed at signing, at whatever the market asks.
what_would_end_it: Mandatory disclosure of market-maker loan terms, or migration to the retainer model where the MM is paid a stablecoin fee and never holds borrowed inventory it owes back to a treasury.
observable: In perps trading far below their own level at listing, buy-side pressure clustering near the 12- and 24-month anniversaries of the listing date, and its absence in perps trading above that level, where the call is exercised against the treasury off-market and no buying ever reaches the book. The listing/delisting table supplies the contract clock; the asymmetry between the two groups is the test, because a generic anniversary effect would hit both.
needs_data_we_lack: The agreements themselves are private - strike, notional and expiry date are not public for any symbol. TGE dates distinct from the Binance perp listing date, and circulating-supply/unlock calendars, are also not held; the listing table is only a proxy for when the contract clock started.
distinct_from: The obligation is contractual redelivery of a borrowed token quantity to a project treasury, not a funding settlement and not a margin call - the MM can be fully solvent and unlevered and still be forced to buy on the day.

payer: the spot-versus-perp arbitrageur whose coin inventory is frozen by a Binance deposit-and-withdrawal suspension for a chain upgrade, while perp trading stays open
why_they_keep_paying: Binance halts deposits and withdrawals on a network at a published wall-clock minute for every hard fork and states explicitly that trading of those tokens is not impacted, then reopens only 'once the upgraded network is deemed to be stable', with no further announcement. The party whose job is to anchor the perp to spot by moving coins between venues therefore cannot replenish, unwind or resize the hedge for a duration nobody knows in advance, and must hold or close at whatever the perp prints.
what_would_end_it: Off-chain settlement of inter-venue transfers (omnibus or custodial-network settlement that does not touch the chain being upgraded), or Binance keeping deposits open through upgrades.
observable: Inside a published suspension window, the perps of tokens on that specific network depart from their own baseline - wider intrabar ranges, a step in the minutes after transfers reopen - while symbols on other networks in the same minutes do not. The window is announced, so the timestamps are exogenous and known before any price is looked at.
needs_data_we_lack: The announcement table (network, affected tokens, suspension start, reopen time) is public but not held in this archive. Measuring the dislocation itself rather than only the perp's own path needs a spot or second-venue price for the same token during the window.
distinct_from: The index feed is healthy and nothing is being force-closed here; what breaks is the physical settlement leg, so the payer is a fully hedged arbitrageur who cannot rebalance, not a mispriced mark or an under-margined position.

payer: the calendar-year-taxed holder who must dispose of a losing position before 31 December to book the loss in that tax year
why_they_keep_paying: A loss is recognised only in the taxable year the disposition occurs - the IRS treats virtual currency as property and requires gain or loss to be reported on the return for the taxable year of the transaction - so the sale is decided by a date rather than by a price. Because the wash-sale rule reaches stock and securities and not property, the same holder may repurchase immediately, which splits the flow into two dated events straddling the boundary instead of one.
what_would_end_it: Extension of the wash-sale rule to digital assets, repeatedly proposed in US legislation; it would remove the reason to complete the sale and the repurchase on opposite sides of 31 December.
observable: Across the year boundaries the archive covers, one-directional pressure in the deepest year-to-date losers during the final sessions of December that reverses in the first sessions of January, with no matching pattern in the same year's winners. The development window holds five such boundaries, so this is five events regardless of how many bars they contain, and the loser/winner split is what separates it from a generic holiday-liquidity effect.
needs_data_we_lack: Nothing extra is needed to measure the calendar pattern - year-to-date rank and the boundary are both in the bars. But nothing in this archive identifies who is taxed where, and US persons are barred from binance.com, so any flow reaching this venue is spillover from where the payer actually trades rather than the payer trading here; that gap cannot be closed with the data held.
distinct_from: The constraint is a statutory reporting year, not a venue rule: this payer holds no leverage, owes no funding, and is not being closed by anyone - they are selling on a date chosen by a tax code.

payer: Ethena's USDe hedging system routing mint and redemption hedges to Binance perpetuals
why_they_keep_paying: Every USDe mint backed by volatile crypto creates delta that Ethena must offset with a short derivative, while every redemption requires the corresponding short to be closed. Maintaining USDe's backing and dollar peg constrains the system to execute these adjustments even when immediate liquidity is costly.
what_would_end_it: Ethena ceasing crypto-backed USDe issuance, replacing volatile backing with stable assets, or allocating no hedges to Binance
observable: BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT should show short-side price pressure and elevated volume during net USDe issuance, with buy-side pressure during net redemptions; the effect should scale with the change in hedged backing allocated to Binance.
needs_data_we_lack: Timestamped USDe mint and redemption flows, historical backing composition, and historical exchange-level hedge allocations
